early_break_fee: No statutory cap on early-termination fees. Any fee must be written into the lease (commonly 1-2 months' rent), and the landlord can only collect actual losses after trying to re-rent — it cannot collect both a fee and rent from a new tenant for the same period.
break_rights: military (SCRA) — Active-duty servicemembers with deployment or PCS orders may end a lease with written notice plus orders; it ends 30 days after the next rent payment is due (50 U.S.C. § 3955).
uninhabitable conditions — If the landlord fails to keep the home habitable, the tenant may give written notice and end the lease if the problem is not fixed within 14 days (Ala. Code § 35-9A-401).
roommate_rules: Roommates who all sign one lease are each responsible for the full rent, not just their share, and one roommate moving out does not end the lease or release them. A name can only be added or removed with the landlord's written agreement, usually when a replacement tenant signs on. One roommate cannot evict another — only the landlord can bring an eviction case.
rent_control_note: No statewide rent control, and state law bans cities and counties from setting rent limits (Ala. Code § 11-80-8.1).

early_break_fee: No statute sets or caps an early-termination fee. Any fee must be in the written lease, and the landlord's claim is limited to actual damages for breaking the agreement (AS 34.03.270).
break_rights: military (SCRA) — Active-duty servicemembers with deployment or PCS orders may end a lease with written notice plus orders; it ends 30 days after the next rent payment is due (50 U.S.C. § 3955).
uninhabitable conditions — If the landlord fails to keep the home habitable, the tenant may give written notice, allow 10 days for repair, and then end the lease (AS 34.03.180).

domestic violence — A tenant who was a victim of domestic violence or sexual assault in the home within the last 30 days may end the lease with written notice plus a protective order or police report, with a move-out date within 30 days and no future rent or fees (ARS 33-1318).
uninhabitable conditions — If the landlord does not fix a material problem within 10 days of written notice (5 days if health or safety is at risk), the tenant may end the lease (ARS 33-1361).

early_break_fee: No statutory cap and no set formula — the lease controls. Because Arkansas landlords generally have no duty to re-rent, a tenant who leaves early can owe rent for the full remaining term unless a buyout or replacement tenant is agreed in writing.
break_rights: military (SCRA) — Active-duty servicemembers with deployment or PCS orders may end a lease with written notice plus orders; it ends 30 days after the next rent payment is due (50 U.S.C. § 3955; Ark. Code Ann. § 12-62-705 for Arkansas National Guard members).

uninhabitable conditions — For leases signed or renewed after Nov. 1, 2021, the home must meet six basic quality standards (water, electricity, sewer, roof, heat/air). The tenant must send written notice by certified mail, stay current on rent, and give the landlord 30 days to fix it before ending the lease (Ark. Code Ann. § 18-17-502).

One roommate cannot evict another — only the landlord can bring an eviction case.
rent_control_note: No statewide rent control, and state law bans local governments from controlling rent (Ark. Code § 14-16-601, strengthened by Act 459 of 2025).

early_break_fee: No statutory cap on early-termination fees. A fee in the lease (typically 1-2 months' rent) must reflect the landlord's actual losses, and the landlord must still try to re-rent, so the tenant usually does not owe the full remaining term.
break_rights: military (SCRA) — Active-duty servicemembers with deployment or PCS orders may end a lease with written notice plus orders; it ends 30 days after the next rent payment is due (50 U.S.C. § 3955).

domestic violence — Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, human trafficking, elder abuse, or certain violent crimes may end a lease with written notice plus proof (protective order, police report, or qualified third-party statement), owing rent for only 14 days after notice (Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.7).

uninhabitable conditions — If the landlord does not fix serious health or safety defects after written notice and a reasonable time, the tenant may move out and end the lease (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1941.1, 1942).

landlord harassment — Repeated illegal entry or serious harassment that makes the home unlivable can support a constructive-eviction claim, but there is no standalone statute and a court decides on the facts.

medical — Tenants age 60 or older, or dependent adults who can no longer live independently, may end a lease to move into a care facility, with written notice and documentation (Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.5).
roommate_rules: Roommates who sign a lease are presumed jointly responsible for the whole rent, not just their share (Cal. Civ. Code § 1659), and moving out does not end that liability — only a written release from the landlord does. A co-tenant cannot evict another co-tenant; only the landlord can file an eviction case, though a roommate who pays more than their share can sue the others for contribution.
rent_control_note: Statewide cap under AB 1482 (Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12): rent may rise no more than 5% plus regional CPI or 10% in 12 months, whichever is lower; 30+ cities including Los Angeles, San Francisco, Oakland, and San Jose also have their own local rent control.

domestic violence — Victims of domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, or human trafficking may end a lease with 3 days' notice and documentation (C.R.S. § 38-12-402).

uninhabitable conditions — If the landlord does not fix a habitability problem after written notice, the tenant may end the lease, withhold rent, or repair and deduct, depending on severity (C.R.S. §§ 38-12-505, 38-12-506).

early_break_fee: No statute caps early-termination fees. A fee in the lease must reasonably reflect the landlord's actual re-renting costs rather than act as a penalty, and the deposit must be applied against what is actually owed.
break_rights: military (SCRA) — Active-duty servicemembers with deployment or PCS orders may end a lease with written notice plus orders; it ends 30 days after the next rent payment is due (50 U.S.C. § 3955).

domestic violence — A tenant who is a victim of family violence or sexual assault and reasonably fears imminent harm may end the lease with 30 days' written notice and no liability for the remaining term (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-11e).
uninhabitable conditions — If the landlord breaches the lease or habitability duties and does not fix the problem within 15 days of the tenant's notice, the lease ends (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 47a-12).

rent_control_note: No statewide cap and no traditional local rent control (barred by case law), but every town of 15,000+ must have a fair rent commission (Conn. Gen. Stat. § 7-148b) that can hear complaints and roll back excessive rents.

early_break_fee: No statutory cap on a fee written into the lease, but if a tenant just leaves, the law caps what is owed at the lesser of the full remaining rent or the rent for the time reasonably needed to re-rent plus re-renting costs (25 Del. C. § 5507(d)).
break_rights: military (SCRA) — Active-duty servicemembers with deployment or PCS orders may end a lease with written notice plus orders; it ends 30 days after the next rent payment is due (50 U.S.C. § 3955; Delaware also has its own Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, 6 Del. C. ch. 25D).
domestic violence — Victims of domestic abuse, sexual offenses, or stalking may end a lease with 30 days' notice (25 Del. C. §§ 5314, 5316).
uninhabitable conditions — If the landlord fails to fix a habitability problem, the tenant may end the lease after 15 days' notice (25 Del. C. § 5306).
job transfer — A job change requiring a move of more than 30 miles allows the tenant to end the lease on 30 days' written notice (25 Del. C. § 5314).
medical — The tenant's serious illness allows the tenant to end the lease on 30 days' written notice (25 Del. C. § 5314).

rent_control_note: No statewide rent cap and no state statute either way on local rent control; no Delaware city has a general rent ordinance in force (only manufactured-home lot rents have justification rules, 25 Del. C. ch. 70).

early_break_fee: An agreed early-termination fee or liquidated damages may not exceed 2 months' rent, the lease may require no more than 60 days' notice, and the tenant must accept it by signing a separate addendum when the lease is made (Fla. Stat. § 83.595(4)). Note: if there is no agreed fee, the landlord may choose to stand by and collect rent as it comes due instead of re-renting.
break_rights: military (SCRA) — Active-duty servicemembers with deployment or PCS orders may end a lease with 30 days' written notice plus orders (Fla. Stat. § 83.682; 50 U.S.C. § 3955).
domestic violence — Victims of domestic violence, dating violence, repeat violence, or sexual violence may end a lease with proof such as a protective injunction (Fla. Stat. § 83.683).
uninhabitable conditions — If the landlord does not fix a material problem within 7 days of written notice, the tenant may end the lease (Fla. Stat. § 83.56).
roommate_rules: On a joint Florida lease every co-tenant is on the hook for the full rent, not just their share, and one roommate leaving does not end the lease or release anyone. A name can only be added or removed with the landlord's written agreement, usually when a replacement tenant signs on. One roommate cannot evict another — only the landlord can file for eviction; a separate per-room lease is the setup that avoids joint liability.
rent_control_note: No statewide rent control, and state law bans local rent control (Fla. Stat. §§ 125.0103, 166.043); the emergency referendum pathway was repealed in 2023.

early_break_fee: No statutory cap on early-termination fees. A fee clause is enforceable only if the loss was hard to estimate in advance, the parties meant it to cover actual damages rather than act as a penalty, and the amount is a reasonable estimate of the landlord's loss; in practice fees run 1-2 months' rent. Georgia landlords generally have no duty to re-rent, so a tenant can owe rent for the full remaining term.

domestic violence — A tenant with a family violence or stalking protective order may end the lease on 30 days' notice and owes only prorated rent (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-23).

uninhabitable conditions — The landlord must keep the home in repair (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-13); if the unit becomes unlivable, the tenant may have a constructive-eviction claim, but there is no simple statutory exit procedure, so get advice before leaving.
